transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I guess the main thing is this constant restless feeling. It’s hard to explain without sounding a little dramatic, but it feels like I’m wound too tight most of the time, like I can’t fully settle into my own body.

Even in situations where I’m supposed to be calm—like sitting through a planning meeting at work, or when I’m painting, or even doing yoga, which is literally meant to help you slow down—I still feel like there’s this motor running inside me. I can be sitting there trying to look composed, but inside I’m just… unsettled. That’s really what brought me in.
Do you find yourself having recurring thoughts that are difficult to stop thinking about?

I’m not sure I’d describe it that way, exactly. I mean, I can get stuck thinking about things, but I don’t know if it’s like… recurring thoughts that feel intrusive or impossible to stop. It’s more that my mind can be busy, and I may replay something from work or a conversation, but I’m not sure that’s what you mean.

When you say recurring thoughts, do you mean like worries that keep coming back even when I don’t want them to, or more like a thought that feels repetitive or upsetting? Because I don’t think I’ve really noticed that as the main problem for me.
Do you ever feel compelled to perform specific rituals or behaviors to relieve your restless feeling?

I don’t think so—not in the way I’d understand “rituals,” at least. I don’t have a particular thing I feel I must do to make the restlessness go away, like a specific sequence or behavior that gives relief.

I mean, I’ll shift around or get up, or I might try to busy myself with something, but that feels more like reacting to being uncomfortable than some ritual I feel compelled to perform. There isn’t a rule in my head like, “If I do this, then the feeling will stop,” if that makes sense.

I guess I’d say I haven’t really noticed anything like that. It’s more just the restless feeling being there, rather than me needing to perform some specific behavior to neutralize it.
Do you have trouble focusing or paying attention to things?

Yes, I think so—though I sometimes hesitate to say “trouble focusing,” because I can sit and work and look like I’m paying attention. But over the past couple of years, I’ve noticed I make more little errors than I used to, especially with detailed things at work.

Like, I’ll go through a vendor spreadsheet and genuinely think I’ve checked it carefully. I’m not just skimming it—I’ll feel like I reviewed it line by line. And then our planning coordinator will catch something I missed, like I transposed a SKU, or I didn’t catch a freight surcharge, or I carried the wrong quantity over into the purchase order. It’s embarrassing, honestly, because those are exactly the kinds of details I’m supposed to be good with in my job.

It’s not every single time, and it’s not like everything is falling apart, but it happens enough that I’ve started second-guessing myself more. I’ll think, “How did I miss that? I looked right at it.”
Do you often find yourself fidgeting or feeling like you need to move when you're supposed to be sitting still?

Yes, definitely. That’s actually one of the things I notice most in situations where I’m supposed to just sit and listen, especially on calls with suppliers.

I’ll be at my desk, and even if I’m following the conversation, my foot is usually bouncing under the desk the whole time. Or I’ll be clicking a pen without realizing it, and then suddenly I notice the sound and think, “Oh gosh, they can probably hear that,” so I have to mute myself. Sometimes I’ll twist my ring over and over, like around my finger, and if it’s a video call I’ll move my hands out of view because I’m aware it probably looks distracting.

It’s not that I’m trying to be rude or impatient. I can be paying attention, but sitting completely still feels… uncomfortable, I guess. Like some part of me has to be moving.
Do you feel like your restless feeling and fidgeting are affecting your relationships or daily activities in a major way?

I wouldn’t say it’s ruining my life or anything that dramatic, but yes, it does affect things in ways I don’t like.

At work, it’s shown up in a practical way. There have been purchase orders I submitted that had to be corrected, and my planning coordinator has started giving them an extra review. She’s very kind about it, but I can tell it’s become a thing—like there’s this extra step now because I might miss something or rush through part of it. And that bothers me, because I’ve always wanted to be seen as reliable and careful.

At home, it’s more interpersonal. Family dinners can get tense because I’ll jump in or respond too quickly, and then people feel like I’m talking over them. I don’t always mean to—I’m not trying to dominate the conversation—but I’ll get caught up and then realize someone looks annoyed or has stopped talking. So it’s not major in the sense that relationships are falling apart, but it definitely creates friction.
Do you often interrupt others or blurt out answers before they've finished speaking?

Yes, I do. Not constantly, but enough that I recognize the pattern.

It happens a lot in vendor negotiations, especially when I think I know where the person is going with a question. They’ll start asking something like, “If we were to adjust the delivery window…” and before they’ve finished, I’m already answering based on what I assume they mean. Then they finish the sentence and there’s some important qualifier I missed—like it only applies to a certain product line, or a smaller quantity, or a different freight arrangement—and I have to back up and say, “Oh, sorry, I misunderstood.” It’s embarrassing because I’m supposed to be listening carefully and negotiating clearly, not jumping ahead.

It also happens when I mentor students in STEM sessions. A student will start asking a question, and I get excited because I think, “Oh, I know exactly what they’re asking,” so I jump in with an explanation. Then I realize they were actually asking a slightly different thing, or there was a detail at the end of the question that changed the whole answer. I don’t mean to cut them off—I’m usually trying to be helpful—but I can tell sometimes I’ve interrupted the flow, and I have to slow myself down and let them finish.
Do you often make impulsive decisions without fully thinking them through?

I’m not sure I’d say “often,” at least not in the sense of making big reckless decisions. I don’t usually do things like suddenly spend a huge amount of money or make major life choices on the spot without thinking.

There are times I decide quickly because I feel like I’ve already understood the situation, especially if it seems straightforward, and then afterward I might realize I should have paused and checked one more detail. But I don’t know if I’d call that impulsive decision-making exactly, or more just… moving too fast sometimes.

So I guess my answer is: not in a major or obvious way that I’ve really noticed. I’d probably need an example of what you mean to be sure.
Did you experience any of these restless or fidgety feelings when you were a child?

Yes, I think so. I mean, it’s a little hard to separate out because it was so long ago, but I do remember in elementary school getting notes sent home for things like popping out of my seat when I wasn’t supposed to, talking over other kids, and answering too quickly before the teacher had even finished asking the question.

I remember that feeling of already knowing—or thinking I knew—what the teacher was going to say, and my hand would shoot up or I’d just say the answer. And then I’d realize I’d interrupted, or the teacher would stop and remind me to wait my turn. It wasn’t like I was trying to be disrespectful. I just felt like I had to get it out right away.

The seat thing stands out too. I wasn’t running around the room constantly, but I’d be up when I was supposed to stay seated—sharpening a pencil, going to look at something, turning around, that kind of thing. Enough that teachers noticed and sent notes home about it.
Do you frequently lose things that you need, like your phone, keys, or documents?

I don’t think so, not frequently. I mean, I misplace things in the normal way—like I’ll set my phone down in the kitchen and then have to think for a second where I left it—but I wouldn’t say it’s a major pattern for me.

Keys and important documents, I’m usually pretty careful with those because I know they matter. I tend to have places where I put them, and if I don’t, I get annoyed with myself pretty quickly and go looking. But I’m not constantly losing things or having it cause big problems.

So… I’d say no, not really. At least not something that stands out to me compared with the other things we’ve talked about.
Do you often have trouble organizing your tasks or activities?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that, because I guess it depends what you mean by organizing. I don’t think of myself as unable to organize tasks, exactly. Like, I can make a list, I can plan out what needs to happen, and at work I generally know what needs to be done.

But I’ll admit I can sometimes make organizing more complicated than it probably needs to be. I’ll start trying to sort out all the steps in my head, or I’ll rearrange the order of things a few times before actually starting, and then I get a little bogged down. But I don’t know if that’s “trouble organizing” in the way you mean, or just me being kind of particular about how I approach things.

If it’s something important, I usually find a way to structure it. I might write things down or group tasks together. So I wouldn’t say it’s a major problem that stands out to me, but I may need an example of what you’re looking for.
Have you experienced these restless and fidgety feelings consistently throughout your life, or have they worsened over time?

It’s been there in some form for as long as I can remember, honestly, but I’d say it’s been noticeably harder to manage more recently.

If I’m trying to put a timeframe on it, probably the last couple of years—maybe a little over two years. Around when the conflicts with my in-laws started taking over more of our evenings, that’s when I noticed I had a harder time settling down. Not that it suddenly appeared out of nowhere, because I do think I’ve always had that restless feeling, but it became more difficult to keep a lid on it.

Before that, I could sort of channel it or manage it well enough most of the time. But over the past, I’d say, about two years and a couple of months, it’s felt more present and harder to calm myself down in the evenings especially, because those situations just seemed to take up so much space.
Do you often act on impulse without considering the consequences of your actions?

Sometimes, yes, though I wouldn’t say I’m doing huge reckless things or anything like that. It’s more like I jump in too quickly before I’ve fully heard something.

For example, in vendor negotiations, someone will be asking a question or laying out a condition, and I’ll start answering before they’ve finished the whole thought. And then a second later I realize, oh, they were adding an important qualifier, or they weren’t actually asking what I thought they were asking. It’s embarrassing because I can usually recover, but it can make me look like I wasn’t listening carefully.

It happens in mentoring sessions too. I do some STEM mentoring, and if someone is asking for help, I’ll sometimes jump in with the answer too fast, before they’ve finished explaining what they’ve tried or what part they’re stuck on. Then I realize I missed a key piece of what they were saying, and I have to back up and say, “Wait, let me make sure I understood that.”

So yes, in that sense I can act impulsively—mostly verbally, jumping ahead—without fully considering that I might be missing something important.
Do you often struggle to complete tasks because you lose focus or get distracted?

I’m not sure I’d describe it that way, at least not as a major pattern. I mean, I do get interrupted or pulled into other things sometimes, like anyone does, but I don’t usually feel like I’m constantly abandoning tasks because I’ve lost focus.

If something doesn’t get finished, it’s more often because the day gets rearranged or something else becomes more urgent, not necessarily because my attention just disappears. I can usually come back to what I was doing, especially if it’s something with a clear deadline or someone else is waiting on it.

That said, I may be defining “distracted” too narrowly. Like, if you mean do I sometimes have to redirect myself or remind myself what I was doing, then yes, probably. But if you mean do I regularly fail to complete things because I can’t stay focused, I don’t think that’s something I’ve noticed as a big issue.
Have you ever been diagnosed with or treated for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder?

No, not that I know of. I’ve never had a formal diagnosis or treatment specifically for that.

I mean, I’ve had moments where I’ve wondered about it, especially as an adult looking back at certain patterns, but I haven’t gone through an evaluation before or been prescribed anything for it. This is really the first time I’m talking through it in this kind of detail with someone.
Do you think your difficulties are more with paying attention to details and following through on instructions, or with feeling restless and impulsive?

I think it’s more the restless and impulsive side, honestly. The reason I’m here is more that constant feeling like I’m wound too tight, like I can’t fully settle myself down even when the situation is supposed to be calm.

Like in a planning meeting, I’m sitting there and outwardly I might look like I’m participating normally, but inside I feel this pressure to move things along or jump in or do something. And it’s not even only at work. It can happen when I’m painting, which is supposed to be relaxing, or even doing yoga, where the whole point is to slow down and be present. I’ll be there thinking, why can’t I just settle into this like everyone else seems to?

So I wouldn’t say my main issue is not understanding instructions or not caring about details. It’s more that I feel keyed up a lot of the time, and that can make me act or speak before I’ve fully paused.
Did you experience these feelings of restlessness and impulsivity consistently throughout your childhood and into your adult years?

Yes, I think it goes back pretty far. I mean, I don’t have a perfect memory of every year, but I do remember in elementary school getting notes sent home because I kept popping out of my seat, talking over classmates, and rushing to answer before the teacher had even finished asking the question.

At the time, I don’t think anyone framed it as anything serious. It was more like, “She needs to wait her turn,” or “She’s too excited,” or “She has trouble staying seated.” And honestly, I probably saw it that way too, like I was just eager or impatient. But looking back, it does feel like the same kind of energy I deal with now, just in a child version.
Have your symptoms of restlessness and impulsivity been present for more than 6 months?

Yes, definitely more than 6 months. The part that feels noticeably harder to manage has been going on for, I’d say, about two years and a couple of months now.

It really seemed to ramp up when the conflicts with my in-laws started taking over more of our evenings. I don’t mean it suddenly appeared out of nowhere, but that’s when it became much more obvious to me that I was having a harder time settling myself and not reacting so quickly. Since then it’s felt pretty consistent, not just a bad week or a short phase.
Have your symptoms of restlessness and impulsivity been present in at least two settings, such as at home, in social situations, or at work?

Yes, definitely in more than one setting. Work is probably the easiest place to point to because there are concrete consequences. I’m a buyer, so when I’m moving too fast or kind of pushing ahead before I’ve fully slowed down, it can show up in purchase orders. I’ve had corrected purchase orders come back, and my planning coordinator has had to put extra review on things because I’ve missed something or acted too quickly. It’s embarrassing, honestly, because I do know what I’m doing, but that restless “just get it done, move it along” feeling gets ahead of me.

And then at home it’s a different version of the same thing. Family dinners can get tense because I jump in too much or talk over people without meaning to. I don’t set out to dominate the conversation, but people feel interrupted, and then the mood shifts. So, yes, it’s not just work or just home—it shows up in both, and other people notice it.
Have your symptoms of restlessness and impulsivity caused significant problems in your relationships or daily life?

Yes, it has. I mean, I wouldn’t say my whole life is falling apart or anything dramatic like that, but it has caused real problems.

At work, it shows up in a way that’s hard to ignore because there’s a paper trail, so to speak. I’ll move too quickly on a purchase order or not slow down enough before sending something through, and then it comes back corrected. My planning coordinator has had to add extra review to my work, which is embarrassing because I do know how to do my job. It’s not that I don’t understand the process. It’s more like I get ahead of myself and then someone else has to catch it.

And at home, it affects relationships more in the moment. Family dinners can get tense because I jump in or talk over people, and even if I don’t mean it that way, people feel interrupted. Then I can see the conversation shift, like everyone gets a little irritated or shuts down. So yes, it’s caused problems both in daily life and in relationships, just in different ways.

If it’s something important, I usually find a way to structure it. I might write things down or group tasks together. So I wouldn’t say it’s a major problem that stands out to me, but I may need an example of what you’re looking for.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms have been persistent since childhood
doctor.question: Have you experienced these restless and fidgety feelings consistently throughout your life, or have they worsened over time?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: It has been noticeably harder to manage for about 2 years and 2 months, since the in-law conflicts started taking over more of our evenings.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the time course of the restless and fidgety feelings, including whether they have been consistent or have worsened over time.

patient.answer:
It’s been there in some form for as long as I can remember, honestly, but I’d say it’s been noticeably harder to manage more recently.

If I’m trying to put a timeframe on it, probably the last couple of years—maybe a little over two years. Around when the conflicts with my in-laws started taking over more of our evenings, that’s when I noticed I had a harder time settling down. Not that it suddenly appeared out of nowhere, because I do think I’ve always had that restless feeling, but it became more difficult to keep a lid on it.

Before that, I could sort of channel it or manage it well enough most of the time. But over the past, I’d say, about two years and a couple of months, it’s felt more present and harder to calm myself down in the evenings especially, because those situations just seemed to take up so much space.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of significant impulsivity in decision-making
doctor.question: Do you often act on impulse without considering the consequences of your actions?

target_item.name: Blurting_Answers
target_item.manifestation: During vendor negotiations or STEM mentoring sessions, I sometimes jump in with an answer before the other person has finished the question, and then I realize I missed an important qualifier.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about impulsive behavior, and this profile most directly reflects acting before fully processing the situation, such as jumping in with an answer before the other person has finished.

patient.answer:
Sometimes, yes, though I wouldn’t say I’m doing huge reckless things or anything like that. It’s more like I jump in too quickly before I’ve fully heard something.

For example, in vendor negotiations, someone will be asking a question or laying out a condition, and I’ll start answering before they’ve finished the whole thought. And then a second later I realize, oh, they were adding an important qualifier, or they weren’t actually asking what I thought they were asking. It’s embarrassing because I can usually recover, but it can make me look like I wasn’t listening carefully.

It happens in mentoring sessions too. I do some STEM mentoring, and if someone is asking for help, I’ll sometimes jump in with the answer too fast, before they’ve finished explaining what they’ve tried or what part they’re stuck on. Then I realize I missed a key piece of what they were saying, and I have to back up and say, “Wait, let me make sure I understood that.”

So yes, in that sense I can act impulsively—mostly verbally, jumping ahead—without fully considering that I might be missing something important.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of significant inattention symptoms
doctor.question: Do you often struggle to complete tasks because you lose focus or get distracted?

target_item.reason: The question asks about failing to complete tasks because of losing focus or being distracted, but the provided symptom profile does not include a matching task-completion or distractibility item.

patient.answer:
I’m not sure I’d describe it that way, at least not as a major pattern. I mean, I do get interrupted or pulled into other things sometimes, like anyone does, but I don’t usually feel like I’m constantly abandoning tasks because I’ve lost focus.

If something doesn’t get finished, it’s more often because the day gets rearranged or something else becomes more urgent, not necessarily because my attention just disappears. I can usually come back to what I was doing, especially if it’s something with a clear deadline or someone else is waiting on it.

That said, I may be defining “distracted” too narrowly. Like, if you mean do I sometimes have to redirect myself or remind myself what I was doing, then yes, probably. But if you mean do I regularly fail to complete things because I can’t stay focused, I don’t think that’s something I’ve noticed as a big issue.

doctor.question: Have you ever been diagnosed with or treated for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder?

target_item.reason: The question asks about prior diagnosis or treatment for ADHD, which is not covered by any listed symptom profile item.

patient.answer:
No, not that I know of. I’ve never had a formal diagnosis or treatment specifically for that.

I mean, I’ve had moments where I’ve wondered about it, especially as an adult looking back at certain patterns, but I haven’t gone through an evaluation before or been prescribed anything for it. This is really the first time I’m talking through it in this kind of detail with someone.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms are primarily inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive
doctor.question: Do you think your difficulties are more with paying attention to details and following through on instructions, or with feeling restless and impulsive?

target_item.name: Feeling_Restless
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is this constant restless feeling, like I’m wound too tight and can’t fully settle, even when I’m supposed to be calmly sitting through a planning meeting, painting, or doing yoga.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the main difficulty is more inattention/detail-follow-through versus restlessness and impulsivity; this profile most directly matches the restlessness side described.

patient.answer:
I think it’s more the restless and impulsive side, honestly. The reason I’m here is more that constant feeling like I’m wound too tight, like I can’t fully settle myself down even when the situation is supposed to be calm.

Like in a planning meeting, I’m sitting there and outwardly I might look like I’m participating normally, but inside I feel this pressure to move things along or jump in or do something. And it’s not even only at work. It can happen when I’m painting, which is supposed to be relaxing, or even doing yoga, where the whole point is to slow down and be present. I’ll be there thinking, why can’t I just settle into this like everyone else seems to?

So I wouldn’t say my main issue is not understanding instructions or not caring about details. It’s more that I feel keyed up a lot of the time, and that can make me act or speak before I’ve fully paused.

doctor.intent: Determine if symptoms have been present since childhood and persisted into adulthood
doctor.question: Did you experience these feelings of restlessness and impulsivity consistently throughout your childhood and into your adult years?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: I remember in elementary school getting notes sent home because I kept popping out of my seat, talking over classmates, and rushing to answer before the teacher finished the question.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the restlessness and impulsivity were present starting in childhood and continuing into adulthood, which directly relates to onset before age 12.

patient.answer:
Yes, I think it goes back pretty far. I mean, I don’t have a perfect memory of every year, but I do remember in elementary school getting notes sent home because I kept popping out of my seat, talking over classmates, and rushing to answer before the teacher had even finished asking the question.

At the time, I don’t think anyone framed it as anything serious. It was more like, “She needs to wait her turn,” or “She’s too excited,” or “She has trouble staying seated.” And honestly, I probably saw it that way too, like I was just eager or impatient. But looking back, it does feel like the same kind of energy I deal with now, just in a child version.

doctor.intent: Determine if symptoms meet criteria for persistence over time
doctor.question: Have your symptoms of restlessness and impulsivity been present for more than 6 months?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: It has been noticeably harder to manage for about 2 years and 2 months, since the in-law conflicts started taking over more of our evenings.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question is directly asking whether the restlessness and impulsivity have lasted longer than 6 months.

patient.answer:
Yes, definitely more than 6 months. The part that feels noticeably harder to manage has been going on for, I’d say, about two years and a couple of months now.

It really seemed to ramp up when the conflicts with my in-laws started taking over more of our evenings. I don’t mean it suddenly appeared out of nowhere, but that’s when it became much more obvious to me that I was having a harder time settling myself and not reacting so quickly. Since then it’s felt pretty consistent, not just a bad week or a short phase.

doctor.intent: Determine if symptoms meet criteria for persistence over time
doctor.question: Have your symptoms of restlessness and impulsivity been present in at least two settings, such as at home, in social situations, or at work?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: At work it has led to corrected purchase orders and extra review from my planning coordinator, and at home it has made family dinners more tense because people feel talked over.
target_item.reason: The question asks whether symptoms are present across at least two settings; this item specifically covers effects at work and at home.

patient.answer:
Yes, definitely in more than one setting. Work is probably the easiest place to point to because there are concrete consequences. I’m a buyer, so when I’m moving too fast or kind of pushing ahead before I’ve fully slowed down, it can show up in purchase orders. I’ve had corrected purchase orders come back, and my planning coordinator has had to put extra review on things because I’ve missed something or acted too quickly. It’s embarrassing, honestly, because I do know what I’m doing, but that restless “just get it done, move it along” feeling gets ahead of me.

And then at home it’s a different version of the same thing. Family dinners can get tense because I jump in too much or talk over people without meaning to. I don’t set out to dominate the conversation, but people feel interrupted, and then the mood shifts. So, yes, it’s not just work or just home—it shows up in both, and other people notice it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the symptoms have caused significant impairment in social, occupational, or other areas of life
doctor.question: Have your symptoms of restlessness and impulsivity caused significant problems in your relationships or daily life?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: At work it has led to corrected purchase orders and extra review from my planning coordinator, and at home it has made family dinners more tense because people feel talked over.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the symptoms have caused significant problems in relationships or daily life, which directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes, it has. I mean, I wouldn’t say my whole life is falling apart or anything dramatic like that, but it has caused real problems.

At work, it shows up in a way that’s hard to ignore because there’s a paper trail, so to speak. I’ll move too quickly on a purchase order or not slow down enough before sending something through, and then it comes back corrected. My planning coordinator has had to add extra review to my work, which is embarrassing because I do know how to do my job. It’s not that I don’t understand the process. It’s more like I get ahead of myself and then someone else has to catch it.

And at home, it affects relationships more in the moment. Family dinners can get tense because I jump in or talk over people, and even if I don’t mean it that way, people feel interrupted. Then I can see the conversation shift, like everyone gets a little irritated or shuts down. So yes, it’s caused problems both in daily life and in relationships, just in different ways.
